reader_summary: A late-Byzantine manuscript of the Greek tragedians; the pages sampled are Euripides' Orestes, Bacchae and Medea. The transcription often does not follow the scribe: on the glossed Orestes page every line is duplicated and most words are invented, and elsewhere whole lines are replaced with plausible-looking Greek. The English translates these errors fluently, drops half of the Medea page, and cannot be used to read the plays.
book_verdict: The scans are good, but the text layer is not usable. A reader would meet invented lines (Zeus as 'murderous' in the Bacchae), duplicated glosses and a half-missing Medea translation.

reader_summary: This is Proclus' commentary on Plato's First Alcibiades, in a clear late manuscript hand, and the transcription is of the right text. But about one line in five is misread at an abbreviation, sometimes changing the argument: a reference to the Phaedo disappears, and a claim about refutation is reversed. The English follows these errors and is not safe to quote without checking against Westerink's edition.
book_verdict: The right work and a readable transcription, but meaning-changing misreads appear on three of four pages, including one sense reversal. Not ready for a Proclus scholar.

reader_summary: This is Kopp's 1826 Greek text of Damascius' Problems and Solutions concerning First Principles. The transcription is accurate, including the Latin footnotes. The English is close and usable, but it leaves out Kopp's Latin notes and the variant readings, and it sometimes drops a clause or flattens a contrast.
book_verdict: The strongest book in this packet: clean OCR and a careful translation. Warn readers that the apparatus is not translated and that there are occasional small omissions.

title: Vitruvii de architectura libri X
shelf_note: A medieval (12th/13th-c.) Laurenziana manuscript of Vitruvius, De architectura; belongs on the classics shelf.
structure_note: A pencilled folio number on each recto (e.g. 54) explains the repeats; backsteps 18 are probably misread pencil numerals. Page 115 is the stained back flyleaf. Its OCR is tagged language 'Arabic' and claims a Kabīkaj invocation and the date 1287; the faint marginal scribbles cannot be read at this resolution, so treat that claim as unverified. Page 30 has a lost lower-left corner (modern paper fill); no text is hidden there.

reader_summary: This is a medieval copy of Vitruvius' De architectura in a heavily abbreviated hand. The transcription is of the right text, but where it expands abbreviations it often invents words: Socrates becomes a 'father-in-law', and the 'southern' peoples become 'Indians'. The English follows those errors, inverts Vitruvius on the southern peoples, and leaves out half of one page.
book_verdict: The manuscript is real and on-shelf, but the text layer misreads abbreviations into invented words and reversed claims. Not showable.
